text: At the saddle, cross to the north side and climb snow until it runs out. From the 7,830 ft saddle the route does not follow the crest: step over onto the snowfield on the north side and climb moderate snow northwest to roughly 8,100 ft. Where the snow ends is the base of the climbing — a couple of hundred feet of third-class rock on the upper east face, reported mostly solid, with cairns marking the stretches where the ground is ambiguous, finishing at the summit. That snow-to-rock transition at about 8,100 ft is the test. If you are still on talus and scree on the south side of the saddle with no snowfield below you, you have not crossed over. If you are working up a broad crest with no snow anywhere, you are on the wrong saddle: the correct one lies due north of the point at which you left the Fisher Creek Trail, between Cosho and Kimtah.

edits.old: step over onto the snowfield on the north side and climb moderate snow northwest to roughly 8,100 ft
edits.new: cross over and work northwest up moderate snow, on the north-side snowfield, to roughly 8,100 ft

text: There are three markers above the lake and they come in order. First, at about 6,800 ft the grade mellows and the trail turns north. Two parties record the same elevation for it. Second, at about 7,600 ft the trail ends — it does not fade, it disappears into a loose gully, and three accounts agree on the height. That is where the scrambling starts. Third, and this is the thing you can see: the gully is marked by a downscoping ribbon of white rock and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it. Negative marker, and it is important because the marking itself is the trap: the paint tempts you straight up that gully. It starts well and turns steep and loose with rolling pebbles higher up. A party who followed the paint up found on the way down that the better line traverses across the gully and around the corner, where cairns lead upward. Once you reach a yellow arrow, the ground improves markedly for the rest of the way. How you know you have finished the hard part, corroborated four ways and genuinely reassuring: the scrambling ends well below the summit and real trail resumes. A mellow path runs the last quarter mile to the top, past the remnants of an old tramway at the top of the cliff section. If you are still scrambling within sight of the summit, you are off the line. There is one false top, a bump on the south ridge, and the trail bypasses it to the west — the real summit sits directly behind it and is not visible from below. Two things to have straight before you go, because both are commonly stated wrongly. The historic lookout stood on the highest summit, not a lower one; the second, lower lookout site is on a peak about a mile east. And the lookout tender here was Gary Snyder in 1952 — Jack Kerouac was on Desolation Peak, a different mountain some fifteen miles away, four years later. The summit register itself carries a card that conflates the two.

edits.old: the gully is marked by a downscoping ribbon of white rock and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it.
edits.new: a ribbon of white rock narrows downward through the gully, and beside it sits the earliest of numerous yellow X's painted on the stone. Once you know what to look for, it is hard to overlook.

text: Northwest Couloir - North Ridge - West Face - South Ridge (per a detailed 2016 account); a 1963 account describes it as a diagonal gully and chimney system to the first notch north of the summit, then a traverse of the ridge and ledges to the summit

edits.old: a 1963 account describes it as a diagonal gully and chimney system to the first notch north of the summit, then a traverse of the ridge and ledges to the summit
edits.new: a 1963 account describes it as a diagonal gully and chimney system that reaches the nearest notch on the north side of the summit, followed by a traverse along the ridge and ledges to the top

text: Cross the glacier from camp to the foot of the northwest couloir and climb it: 40-45 degrees of snow, usually simul-climbed on pickets or flukes, and three to four hours of it. Above the couloir a narrow snow-and-rock gully gains the north ridge, then an exposed traverse around a line of pinnacles on loose Class 4-5 ledges leads to the headwall — a short, near-vertical crack at 5.8+ (or 5.2/A1). Ledges on the upper west face above it lead onto the south summit ridge. Treat every hold on the ridge as suspect and budget hard for the descent, because parties routinely run out of daylight here and end up bivouacking.

edits.old: then an exposed traverse around a line of pinnacles on loose Class 4-5 ledges leads to the headwall
edits.new: then an exposed traverse on loose Class 4-5 ledges skirts a row of pinnacles and arrives at the headwall

text: At the top of the headwall that bars the upper west face, immediately beyond the band of giant boulders. The headwall runs from the ridge crest down to a lower cliff band and forms a near-impasse; the crossing is the roughly 10-ft vertical crack, the third of four lines evaluated across it — the ridge crest, a high catwalk ledge, this crack, and the bottom nose. Reached on the way down after downclimbing the summit ridge and the loose ledges below it.

edits.old: The headwall runs from the ridge crest down to a lower cliff band and forms a near-impasse;
edits.new: The headwall spans the distance between the crest of the ridge and a cliff band below, and it nearly blocks the way;

text: A small horn draped with several rappel slings, on the exposed traverse around the north ridge's pinnacles. It is passed on the way UP, between the notch at the top of the couloir and the easier ground beyond, on loose class 4-5 ledges — note it on the ascent, because it is the descent anchor.

edits.old: A small horn draped with several rappel slings, on the exposed traverse around the north ridge's pinnacles.
edits.new: A small horn wearing a number of rappel slings, found along the exposed traverse past the pinnacles of the north ridge.

text: Descent goes down Green Drag-on then swings left into Rise and Fall; clipping a bolt as a directional makes the pendulum easier

edits.old: then swings left into Rise and Fall; clipping a bolt as a directional makes the pendulum easier
edits.new: then swings left into Rise and Fall; the pendulum goes more easily if you clip a bolt for direction

text: Continue up the Davis-Holland: fingers and thin hands in a right-facing corner to a two-bolt anchor on a sloping ledge. This is the most gear-hungry pitch. With some backcleaning it links with the next pitch into one long 55 m pitch of 5.10.

edits.old: fingers and thin hands in a right-facing corner to a two-bolt anchor on a sloping ledge
edits.new: a right-facing corner takes fingers and thin hands, ending at a two-bolt anchor on a ledge that slopes

text: Look up and right for a lone black-hangered bolt. Undercling the roof as for the right variation of Davis-Holland, reach a jug under the bolt, then a short tricky section (horizontal takes a #2 Camalot) leads onto the second pitch of Rise and Fall. Skip the belay out right, clip the next black bolt up-left, and follow crystal edges up a dike; the crux is getting past two roofs at the end. Three-bolt belay.

text: Up the corner on thin gear to a good jug, then clip the shiny bolt out right (the bolts up and left belong to Green Drag-on). A balancy section leads to a tenuous second clip, then powerful moves work right past the third bolt to the three-bolt Town Crier anchor. Bouldery and fun.

text: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the long pullout on the north side of the road about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, roughly half a mile west of the Blue Lake Trailhead. The climbers' track leaves the east end of the pullout. SR-20 over Washington Pass is closed in winter, typically from late fall until spring.

edits.old: to the long pullout on the north side of the road about 1.5 miles west
edits.new: to the lengthy pullout beside the road's north edge, about 1.5 miles west

text:
From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' track from its east end down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak. Then traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak, where the East Face routes begin.

Avoid the steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall on the way in.

edits.old: Then traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak, where the East Face routes begin.
edits.new: Next, cross the rib running south off the South Buttress and enter the basin lying east of Cutthroat Peak, which is the start of the East Face routes.

text: Traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak. That second basin is where the East Face routes begin. So the count is two basins, and the rib between them is the thing you cross: first the basin below the peak's south side, which is where the South Buttress and North Ridge parties go, then over a rib, then the east basin. If you have not crossed a rib, you are still in the south basin and you are under the wrong side of the mountain. The negative test against the North Ridge, which leaves the same boulder field: that route bears right and north into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch, and gains it by a loose runout 5.7 pitch. If you are roping up for a single hard pitch to reach a notch, you are on the North Ridge, not on the East Face. A hazard that is also a route-finding instruction, and it is stated in both routes on this side: avoid the steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall on the way in. If your line into the base is up a confined chimney full of scree, you have picked the wrong way through and should back out and go round. There is no named crack or flake at the start; the basin, the rib and the chimneys to avoid are the ground features to go by. Descent: parties commonly descend the South Buttress with multiple rappels, or the West Ridge on fixed-anchor rappels plus downclimbing, rather than reversing the technical face.

edits.old: Traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak.
edits.new: Cross the rib running south off the South Buttress and drop into the basin lying east of Cutthroat Peak.

text: Drive SR-20 to the long pullout on the north side of the highway about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, at roughly 5,200 ft. The climbers' track leaves the east end of that pullout — it starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past. It is genuinely hard to find in the dark, so spend a minute at the east end before committing to a pre-dawn start.

edits.old: Drive SR-20 to the long pullout on the north side of the highway about a mile and a half west
edits.new: Drive SR-20 to the lengthy pullout beside the north edge of the highway, about a mile and a half west

text: Climb the left side of the gully to the ridge crest, then about 12 pitches up to 5.8 along the buttress, past a chockstone crawl, a stembox crux and an offwidth near the false summit. Drop off the false summit and climb the final pitch to the true summit.

edits.old: Climb the left side of the gully to the ridge crest, then about 12 pitches
edits.new: Follow the gully's left side up to the crest of the ridge, then continue about 12 pitches

text: A single rack from 0.3 to 3 inches sews up the crux pitches; a few doubles in the 0.5-2 range stitch the whole route. An optional #4 protects the short summit-ridge offwidth. Bring lots of single and double-length runners. A single 60m rope suffices for the descent.

edits.old: A single rack from 0.3 to 3 inches sews up the crux pitches; a few doubles in the 0.5-2 range stitch the whole route.
edits.new: One set of gear from 0.3 to 3 inches protects the crux pitches, and the entire route goes with a handful of doubles between 0.5 and 2.

text:
Park in the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass. The trail leaves from the east end of that pullout and drops straight into the woods; the climbers' track actually starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the pullout's eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past.

The path drops through timber, crosses State Creek — fill up, it is the last reliable water — and then climbs steadily up into the big meadow and basin below Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half from the car to the foot of the entry gully.

Above the meadow the trail steepens into a boulder field beneath the south buttress.

edits.old: The trail leaves from the east end of that pullout and drops straight into the woods; the climbers' track actually starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the pullout's eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past.
edits.new: The trail heads off from the pullout's east end and plunges directly into the woods. In practice the climbers' track begins just west of a clump of trees near that eastern end; cairns usually mark it, yet on a first visit you may have to search, and it is simple to stroll right by.

text: Climb hollow rock below a roof and place gear carefully, then move left to a pedestal, up the left-facing dihedral, and exit right. Belay at the bolted anchor next to a dead tree on a large flat ledge.

edits.old: Belay at the bolted anchor next to a dead tree on a large flat ledge.
edits.new: Belay from the bolted anchor beside a dead tree, on a big flat ledge.

text: Climb easy blocky ground, traverse about 20 ft right into a chimney, exit onto a ledge, then traverse about 15 ft left. Climb a short seam on small gear to a large ledge with a tree and a cave.

edits.old: Climb a short seam on small gear to a large ledge with a tree and a cave.
edits.new: Climb a short seam with small gear, reaching a large ledge that holds a tree and a cave.

text: From the saddle at the foot of the west ridge, traverse ledges east along the south face about 100 ft to a shallow, blocky gully. Scramble the lower gully (Class 3-4, mostly solid), then belay the last section up to the ridge crest past two fixed pitons; a double-bolt station sits in the gully. Do not take the second, harder southwest gully by mistake.

edits.old: traverse ledges east along the south face about 100 ft to a shallow, blocky gully. Scramble the lower gully
edits.new: work eastward across ledges on the south face for about 100 ft until you reach a shallow, blocky gully. Scramble up its lower part

text: At the summit block, traverse an obvious ledge across its northwest face to the upper North Ridge. A wide ledge at the base gives room to belay. One belayed pitch of low 5th-class rock on good holds, then easy scrambling, reaches the top. The first rappel station is just west of the summit.

edits.old: At the summit block, traverse an obvious ledge across its northwest face to the upper North Ridge.
edits.new: Where the summit block begins, follow a clear ledge across its northwest face to reach the upper North Ridge.

text: Below the upper rappels the ridge flattens out. The continuation is down the crest and then onto third-class ledges on the south side of the ridge; the next bolted station sits above the large dihedral that dominates this part of the west side.

edits.old: then onto third-class ledges on the south side of the ridge;
edits.new: then over to third-class ledges along the ridge's south side;

text: From Dayton, follow North Touchet Road out of town toward Ski Bluewood; it is paved for roughly the first 15 to 16 miles, then turns to gravel as Forest Service Road 64 at the national forest boundary. The Dikes sit along that road in the East Fork Touchet River valley below Ski Bluewood, in the Walla Walla Ranger District of the Umatilla National Forest. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. You do not park at this trailhead: for Megadike South, keep driving about 1.2 miles further south on FR 64 past it and pull off on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river.

edits.old: keep driving about 1.2 miles further south on FR 64 past it and pull off on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river.
edits.new: continue roughly 1.2 miles beyond it, southbound on FR 64, and stop at a pullout on either shoulder shortly ahead of the river bridge.

text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike South: drive 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and park on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river. Scramble up the steep hillside on the NW side of the road above the bridge abutment, then continue uphill along the dike to a passable gully.

edits.new: the south Megadike is reached by leaving the car near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, then scrambling straight up the steep slope over the bridge abutment

edits.new: go 1.2 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and pull over on either shoulder shortly before the river bridge. Climb the steep slope that rises northwest of the road, above the bridge abutment,

text: Dark Peak is regarded as an adventure/remoteness objective more than a technically hard one. After a boat-and-shuttle approach into the roadless Stehekin Valley, parties hike the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT) to a high camp, then leave the trail for a long, routefinding-heavy cross-country push -- either up the historically brushy, officially abandoned Swamp Creek climbers' path, or via a newer variant farther south on the PCT to Hemlock Camp -- gaining a basin below "Dark Fin Col." From the col, parties rope up, descend a loose slope onto the crevassed Dark Glacier, pick a line across it (the right side of the glacier is reported as a good line), and finish with a belayed crossing of the summit moat/bergschrund onto the rock ridge leading to the top. Reported early-to-mid-summer conditions give firm, well-bridged snow with minimal crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are exposed and the glacier becomes less stable.

text: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.

edits.new: and the route then goes up steep forest that bends rightward at its top into a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Past that is another, higher basin near 5,500 ft, under the slabs left by the shrinking glacier.

text: The headwall has a tempting wrong line on it, and the glacier has a tempting wrong line above it. Coming up the basin the headwall looks formidable; the way up is at its far left, through a brushy gully where the headwall corners, and there is an appetising forested cut up the wall to the right of the waterfall that must not be taken — cutting right early forces you onto the low end of the rock wall in the trees. Above, steep forest veers right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft, where a piece of orange flagging has marked the way. Beyond that, a third and higher basin near 5,500 ft sits below the slabs of the receding glacier, and a natural cut on that basin's southwest side leads through the slabs onto the ice: easy snow early in the season, later a gully with a stream in it. Once on the glacier, the second trap: a snow and talus slope under the north side of the summit looks enticing and leads to the northeast ridge, which is far more exposed and saves nothing. Do not take it.

text: Open forest and slopes, not brush, is the sign you are on this variant. Leaving the crest trail farther south, the climb northwest gains roughly 3,500 ft through timber and open slope that stays walkable; if you are fighting slide alder and vine maple you have started up the Swamp Creek drainage instead and are on the older, much harder line. Veer left near the top of the drainage to reach the drop-in point onto the glacier — parties have needed a rappel to get off the ridge here, so carry the means to do it. Once on the ice, ignore the snow and talus slope running up under the north side of the summit: it looks enticing from the glacier and leads to the northeast ridge, which is much more exposed and saves no time. Leave the glacier by crossing the moat onto the rock instead, then take the three step-ups — up and left, up and left, up and left — to gain the west spur around 8,200 ft, east of the actual saddle.

text: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of Dark Peak continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. The approach is all of the difficulty. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.

text: Jam the hand crack at the far left of the upper walls, where the approach trail arrives. It is often damp even when the rest of the route is dry; stemming off the left wall helps on the slippery opening layback. From the ledge, wander right and then back left over small terraces to a bolted belay in a right-facing corner.

text: Turn into Diablo at milepost 126. Older directions run you to the northernmost street and across a lawn to find the unmarked Stetattle Creek trail on the east bank of the creek; this is a quiet residential neighbourhood, so bypass the houses and drive the lakeshore past the powerhouse to the large public parking lot with restrooms built for the Seattle City Light dam tours, and walk the extra distance. Since the climb finishes at the Gorge Creek bridge at about milepost 123, leave a shuttle car there.

There is no trail: the route leaves the highway directly.

text: Late spring is the consensus best window. Snow still suppresses the salal and slide alder, snowmelt provides water on a slope that otherwise has none, and avalanche danger on the south side is minimal. Mid-summer turns an entirely south-facing 6,000-ft slope into an oven and the brush reaches full leaf; late summer and fall add a genuine water problem on top of that. Winter ascents have been made — one party climbed it over the first weekend in January, camping in sub-zero weather (down to -22F) and passing huge cornices, and reported that the brush at least was minimised. With light bivy gear and no-cook food in warm spring weather, one party found it very pleasant, which is the strongest endorsement this route gets.

edits.new: In warm spring weather, one party carried minimal bivy gear and food needing no cooking, and found the outing very pleasant,

text: There is no trailhead in the usual sense — you step off the highway into the forest. Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem near milepost 123, or about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge. There are parking lots at each end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles, so park at the west lot. Elevation here is 1,096 ft, and there are accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the Gorge Creek Falls viewpoint. Walk across the bridge to its east end, go a few feet farther east, cross the highway, and pick the easiest place to start uphill into the woods. That is the whole approach: the route and the approach are the same thing from here, 6,000 vertical feet of it. Round trip is about 6.2 miles with roughly 6,000 ft of gain in three miles. Carry water. The slope is south-facing and dry once the snow is gone, and there is no reliable source between the highway and the snowfields high on the mountain. In late spring, snowmelt on the route solves this and simultaneously suppresses the brush, which is why that window is the usual recommendation.

text: Feasible in one very long day or, more comfortably, as an overnight. Day trip: leave the Gorge Creek bridge before dawn; the South Davis saddle at 5,700 ft is about 4.4 hours from the car and the summit about 8.3 hours; allow 4.1 hours down, for roughly 13.5 hours car to car and 10 miles travelled with about 7,400 ft gained and lost if you take the Gorge Creek/South Buttress line with its detours. The round-trip figure for the direct line is 6.2 miles. Overnight: one party camped at the 5,720+ ft saddle, where there was room for two tents on a snow ledge; what is there when the snow has melted is not documented. That splits the trip into a long brushy climb on day one and a short summit push plus the full descent on day two, and it is the version to choose if you are unsure of the slab above the saddle. An overnight requires a wilderness permit.

text: Deep Blue begins on a fin-like flake right off the ground — mount the flake and pull a small bulge into easier climbing. Lower/mid pitches include an overhang leading into face climbing to a small ledge below a roof, a pitch through a roof with technical edges to a ledge, and a stretch of 5.11 climbing to a higher ledge below the crux. Higher up, steep 5.10+ lieback flakes lead to an alcove, then a roof with a bouldery V6 crux on perfect edges (~25m pitch), before steep, sequential climbing on good holds leads toward the 5.13c crux pitch itself (~35m, sustained overhanging climbing to a vertical-face crux) and a further 5.12 pitch (~35m) through another roof. The route was developed over several years and finished in 2020; it climbs in 12 pitches with link-up options for parties wanting to move faster, and multiple parties have completed it car-to-car in a day without simul-climbing.

text: From Bird Creek Camp (~4,200 ft) on the Devore Creek Trail, traverse to open meadows and a waterfall cirque, then climb semi-open slopes and snow ramps into the ~7,000 ft basin between Wy'North Peak and Devore Peak (the Bird Lakes basin). Cross Bird Creek at the northern lake and hike southeast up talus/scree to a col at roughly 7,500 ft on Devore's southeast ridge. From the col, scramble west along Class 3 terrain, working past a false summit block, to an unavoidable ~20-ft rock step (Class 5.0-5.4) just below the true summit; a short final Class 3-4 pitch tops out at the 1940 first-ascent register.

text:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.

text: From the Downey Creek Campground trailhead (~1,450 ft) on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), take the Downey Creek Trail #768, staying on the east bank of Downey Creek through old-growth forest. The trail is rough and lightly maintained — expect brush, downed timber, and washed-out sections; a footlog or ford may be needed at Bachelor Creek (~6.5 mi in), which has been scoured by past avalanches that swept debris across the valley and buried sections of trail. Beyond Bachelor Creek the trail climbs steeply out of the valley toward Cub Lake, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft from the trailhead; this stretch crosses open avalanche paths below Spire Point that should be assessed for stability in early-season snow. Camp is typically made in meadows southeast of Cub Lake (~5,300 ft) or, better positioned for summit day, up on the ridge above at ~6,200 ft (add ~1 hr from the lake). Reported car-to-camp time is 9-11 hours given the distance, brush, and elevation gain — budget this as a genuine multi-day approach, not a day hike-in. From high camp, a boot path crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, then the route drops ~200 ft and traverses cross-country (roughly 80° bearing) below cliff bands, over glacier-polished slabs (bare rock in late season, snow-covered early season) and a boulder/snow slope, to gain the base of the Dome Glacier. This traverse is unmarked route-finding on exposed, sometimes loose terrain — a map/compass or GPS track is strongly recommended.

text: The namesake flake sits about 6 m above the talus at the nearest point of the far western wall. Boulder up sculpted knobs to the flake's lower edge, where a good crack takes a range of sizes, and stem over the lip. A 4-inch cam in the top of the flake protects knobs to a bolt; step right up cracks and ledges past another bolt, then back left via a quartz-studded block to a big ledge and smear past two bolts to the anchor.

text: Step down and left from the sharp ridge onto a large ledge, then scramble back to the crest and follow it to a small saddle below the Fin. The rock is lichen-covered and loose in places, with several possible lines; most parties simul-climb this section, keeping to the left side of the ridge where the choice is unclear. Watch rope drag and loose blocks.

text:
Identical to the Serpentine approach as far as the moraine: Stuart Lake Trailhead, left at the junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, about four miles and 2,280 ft to Colchuck Lake — roughly an hour and a half of uphill from the trail junction. Fill water and use the toilet near the lake's south end; there is nothing above.

Past the campsites you drop out of the forest into large talus blocks and follow cairns, then pick up the climbers' path along the moraine, passing a small creek on your left, until the face opens up in front of you.

A perennial snow patch sits below the start; its size varies year to year and it is usually short enough that crampons and axe are a convenience rather than a necessity by midsummer. Above it, a loose gully and gravel ledges lead to the scrambling.

Parties report roughly four and a half to five and a half hours from car to the first roped pitch.

text: Follow the trail along the lake's west shore, across the boulder field at the south end and around to the inlet below Aasgard Pass, then climb the cairned path up the pass, about 2,200 ft in three quarters of a mile. Stay left: a few hundred feet up the path crosses to the left of the creek, and at about 6,400 ft keep left of the small cliff band with the waterfall and ignore side paths toward it.

text:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft of gain.

From the lake's west side follow the cairned climbers' path up Aasgard Pass, gaining roughly 2,200 ft in about three quarters of a mile.

The pass itself is where people get hurt, and the rule is simple: stay left. A few hundred feet above the lake the path crosses to the climber's left of the creek and stays there. At the first grove of larches keep well clear to the left of the rock, in any season. At about 6,400 ft stay left of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it and ignore every side path leading toward the waterfall — deaths are on record on that side, and the right-hand ground cliffs out.

From the top of the pass head right and south along a short ridge above a tarn to reach Dragontail's east saddle, then cross the Snow Creek Glacier basin — a mellow slope with little crevassing, snow-covered through most of the summer — to the saddle on the east ridge.

text: Also called the North Face route. First climbed in summer as mostly 4th/low-5th class rock with a couple of 5.7 cruxes; in recent years it has become a sought-after winter/spring alpine ice and mixed objective, following snow ramps just right of the low point of the face and then the runnels splitting the dark rock band two-thirds up. Winter conditions are highly variable with multiple line options; in good nick it's described as offering more sustained exposure than the neighboring Triple Couloirs.

text: Climbs an obvious dihedral system past two trees with webbing to a large terrace, then crack systems and a small dihedral to the crux — two consecutive 5.8 pitches (a finger crack into a splitter hand crack, then a dihedral with bomber finger locks) that can be linked with a 70m rope. Above the crux the route stays on the ridge crest with mostly 3rd-4th class/low-5th scrambling, a short downclimb, and a sandy gully to the summit area. All of the technical climbing is on solid rock even though the low-5th-class sections are loose.

text: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.

text: Four rappels plus downclimbing, on a single 60 m rope, using the standard summer bolted stations down the west side to the North/South Early Winters Spire notch, then the piton-and-nut anchor in the skier's-right wall to get past the West Couloir chockstone. The competing figure of about six belongs to a different line: a newer, fully bolted rappel route down the right side of the West Face, roughly six stations spaced about 100 ft (30 m) apart. That line does not include the chockstone rappel; a 60 m rope only just works on it, and on its third station you have to reach down to clip in before letting the rope run through, so knot the ends. Do not mix stations between the two lines.

edits.old: then the piton-and-nut anchor in the skier's-right wall to get past the West Couloir chockstone.
edits.new: and after that an anchor of pitons and nuts, set in the wall on skier's right, gets you past the West Couloir chockstone.
